articles.description:
TL;DR: I spent 3 months researching image-based attacks after a security incident. What I found was alarming: standard "metadata stripping" does almost nothing against modern threats. The only mathematical guarantee of safety is completely destroying and rebuilding the image from scratch.
Last year, a friend's startup got hacked. The attack vector? A user's profile picture.
Not a PDF. Not an executable. A simple JPEG uploaded through their avatar picker.
The file passed every standard check:
✅ File extension: .jpg

✅ MIME type: image/jpeg

✅ Magic bytes: Valid (FF D8 FF...)
✅ Antivirus: Clean
✅ Metadata stripped with ExifTool
They were still compromised.
I spent the next three months going down the rabbit hole of polyglots and steganography. What I found changed how I handle user uploads f…
articles.title: I Discovered Why "Stripping Metadata" From Images is Security Theater 🎭

articles.description:
You're doing a rolling deployment. Half your instances are running v1, half are
The expand and contract pattern prevents this.
Traditional migrations assume all application instances update simultaneously.
-- This breaks rolling deployments
ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name;

The moment this runs, every v1 box querying name fails.
Expand and contract splits breaking changes into backward-compatible steps:
Expand: Add the new structure alongside the old one
Migrate: Dual-write in application code, backfill existing data
Contract: Remove the old structure once nothing uses it
Each step is a separate deployment. Each deployment is safe to run while both

articles.description:
"I asked ChatGPT to make a login feature, but it gave me weird code."
I hear this complaint frequently lately. GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude... AI tools are flooding in, but production-ready code isn't coming out.
Is AI the problem? No.
The problem is how we communicate with AI.
Let's look at a real case.
"Make a login feature"
def login(username, password):
    if username == "admin" and password == "password":
        return {"status": "success"}
    return {"status": "failed"}

"What is this? AI is not good..."
Wait, who made the mistake here?
What happens if you just tell a junior developer "make a login feature"?
You'll probably get questions like:
"What framework should I use?"
"What database?"
"Session? JWT?"
"Social login too?"
"Any password rules?"
But AI doesn't ask questions. …
